## A natural laboratory for Europe: lessons from the Alpujarra

On the southern slopes of Sierra Nevada, the landscape changes with a rapidity rarely found on the European continent. From the subtropical crops of the Órgiva plain to the perpetual snowfields of Mulhacén, a journey of some sixty kilometers traverses four complete bioclimatic zones. This altitudinal compression turns the Alpujarra into a real-scale laboratory: processes that take centuries to manifest in other mountain ranges can be observed here in decades.

The Sierra Nevada Global Change Observatory, attached to the Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas, has been using this gradient for years as a sentinel of the Mediterranean climate. Its researchers have deployed twelve automatic stations along the altitudinal transect, from three hundred meters above sea level in the Guadalfeo valley to three thousand three hundred meters at the summits. Each station records temperature, humidity, solar radiation, and precipitation on an hourly basis, generating time series that allow what happens in each bioclimatic zone to be compared with unusual precision.

The logic of the observatory is as simple as it is powerful: if global warming shifts bioclimatic zones upward, what happens today at a thousand meters in altitude anticipates what will happen tomorrow at twelve hundred. The data collected in the Alpujarra serve to calibrate models that are then applied to the Apennines, the Dinaric Alps, or the Atlas Mountains. Mountain regions that lack such a compact gradient find in Sierra Nevada an empirical reference to predict how their ecosystems will respond to rising temperatures.

One of the most relevant findings of the observatory concerns the speed of change. The time series show that the lower limit of high mountain vegetation has risen detectably over the last two decades. Species that once found their thermal optimum at eighteen hundred meters now thrive at two thousand one hundred, while the plant communities at the summits see their living space reduced. This phenomenon, documented in the observatory's own scientific publications, has turned the Alpujarra into a case study cited in international forums on climate change adaptation.

The uniqueness of the Alpujarra transect lies not only in its thermal gradient. The southern orientation of the slope, the influence of the Mediterranean Sea less than forty kilometers away in a straight line, and summer aridity create conditions that are not replicated in any other European mountain. CSIC researchers describe it as a natural analog of what climate change could impose on other mountainous regions of southern Europe in the coming decades. The Alpujarra is not an exceptional case to be studied out of scientific curiosity: it is a mirror in which other regions can see their own future.

The observatory's automatic stations have also recorded an increase in interannual variability. Winters tend to be shorter and springs more erratic, with episodes of early heat that advance flowering and late frosts that damage woody crops. This instability, measured precisely along the Alpujarra gradient, offers practical lessons for water management and agriculture throughout the Mediterranean basin. The data do not remain on the CSIC servers: they are shared with the irrigation community, with the technicians of the Junta de Andalucía, and with the municipalities of the region.

The value of the observatory as a European scientific infrastructure has grown as the data series accumulate. What began as a local monitoring project has become a reference for continental research programs. Teams from German, Italian, and French universities request access to the time series to validate their own models. The Alpujarra, known for centuries for its isolation and subsistence economy, has transformed into a climate knowledge node with international reach.

This scientific dimension coexists with the daily life of the region without major friction. The automatic stations, discreet and powered by solar panels, go unnoticed by most visitors. The shepherds who take their livestock up to the mountains in summer know their location and, in some cases, collaborate with researchers by reporting observations on plant phenology or the presence of species at unusual altitudes. This local knowledge, passed down from generation to generation, complements the instrumental records with a perspective that no machine can capture.

The Sierra Nevada Global Change Observatory publishes periodic reports summarizing the state of the Alpujarra gradient. The latest available documents point to an unequivocal trend: average annual temperatures have risen in all bioclimatic zones, with more pronounced increases at higher altitudes. Precipitation, for its part, shows a slight decrease in spring and an increase in torrential episodes in autumn. These patterns, consistent with the projections of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change for the western Mediterranean, reinforce the role of the Alpujarra as an early warning system.

The lesson the region offers to Europe is not only scientific. The Alpujarra demonstrates that a rural territory can host top-level research infrastructure without renouncing its identity. The white villages, the centuries-old irrigation channels, and the cultivated terraces continue to function while the automatic stations record data that feed global climate models. This coexistence between tradition and cutting-edge science constitutes, in itself, a valuable lesson for other mountain regions seeking to adapt without losing their character.

CSIC researchers insist that the Alpujarra gradient is a non-renewable resource in scientific terms. Every year that passes without records is a year lost forever, a gap in the time series that no model will be able to reconstruct. That is why the observatory maintains a rigorous maintenance program and an open data policy that guarantees the continuity of the measurements. The Alpujarra, without intending to, has become a European scientific heritage as valuable as its landscapes or its vernacular architecture.

The sixty kilometers that separate the Guadalfeo valley from the summits of Sierra Nevada condense a climatic history that the rest of the continent is only just beginning to glimpse. What happens in this corner of Andalucía does not stay on its slopes: it travels in the form of data, publications, and models to offices in Brussels, laboratories in Munich, and research centers in Montpellier. The extreme Alpujarra, with its four climates in sixty kilometers, has earned a place on the map of European science without needing to give up anything that makes it unique.
